finding.claim: dropTable ignores the error returned by Authorize, so any caller reaches the DROP TABLE regardless of role. The table name is also concatenated into the SQL string with no allowlist, so it allows SQL injection.
finding.source: Any user who reaches /admin/drop, with no 'dba' role needed. The table name comes from the request form value 't' (r.FormValue("t")).

trace.note: /admin/drop is registered with http.HandleFunc and has no auth middleware
Authorize(u, "dba") returns a 'forbidden' error, but the return value is discarded and execution continues
Unvalidated r.FormValue("t") is concatenated into the DROP TABLE statement and passed to runSQL

finding.guards_checked: Authorize is the only guard, and its result is not enforced (unlike vacuum, which checks err and returns 403). No middleware wraps the route. There is no table-name allowlist or parameterization. runSQL is a stub in this file, but it is the SQL execution sink by name. userFrom does an unchecked type assertion on the context value, which would panic if no user was set. That is a robustness issue, not an authorization bypass.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 is the only guard, but its error return is discarded, so it has no effect. There is no middleware, allowlist or parameterization.
verdict.reason: api.go:26 calls Authorize as a bare statement and discards its error, unlike vacuum at api.go:33, so any caller with a user in context reaches the concatenated DROP TABLE at api.go:27, and the table name is unvalidated. Caveat: nothing in this repo sets the "user" context value (the only match is the read at api.go:22), so the type assertion would panic here unless external middleware sets it. That assumption is the same one vacuum relies on, so the missing role check still holds.
